title: 28 Observations About the State of AI in Schools
author: Eric Hudson
summary: A school AI consultant compiles 28 field notes from a year of trainings, student panels, and school visits into a snapshot of where K-12 AI policy and practice actually stand, well past the headline debates. His throughline is that most schools are stuck in a deficit model — telling students and staff what they can't do with AI, with no parallel guidance on productive use — and that "traffic light" AI policies are proving hard to enforce or keep current, prompting a shift toward two-lane assessment models and co-constructed student guidelines. He repeatedly contrasts how fast students learn AI informally from peers and social media against how cautiously adults learn from mainstream media, and flags that educators' preference for research over power users is a liability when so much AI research is already outdated or irrelevant to K-12 contexts by the time it's published. A sharp methodological point involves AI detectors: he shows a clean Pangram scan of an essay he wrote entirely himself but drafted through a 25,000-word interaction with Claude, arguing detectors can flag pasted AI text but cannot detect AI influence on human-written work. He closes by reframing the central question schools ask from "can AI do this?" to "should AI do this?", and argues the ongoing techlash and disagreement about AI in schools is a healthy feature of institutions resisting binary thinking, not a problem to be resolved.
points: AI policies in schools continue to operate from a pure deficit model — spelling out what students and staff cannot do with AI, with no matching guidance on approved or encouraged uses — which the author argues undermines motivation to actually learn the technology.

"Traffic light" AI guidelines are proving hard to enforce and keep updated, pushing schools toward alternatives like two-lane assessment models, explicitly AI-infused courses, and guidelines co-constructed with students.

Students learn AI fast and informally from peers and social media; adults learn slower and more cautiously from mainstream media and colleagues, and are "more reluctant to share with each other" — a knowledge-transfer gap schools haven't solved.

AI detectors can only tell you whether AI-generated text was pasted in, not whether AI meaningfully shaped human-written work — demonstrated by a clean Pangram scan of an essay the author wrote himself after a 25,000-word Claude conversation used for brainstorming and editing.

The Rithm Project's survey of 2,600 teenagers found "non-judgmental intergenerational conversation may be the most important intervention available" — reframing the school AI problem as a relational/communication gap as much as a policy one.
quotes: In general, AI policies continue to operate from a deficit model, communicating solely what students and employees cannot do with AI while offering no guidance or encouragement about ways it could be helpful to them or uses the school would approve of.

I'm seeing a gradual realization in schools that "traffic light" models of AI guidelines are hard to enforce and to keep updated. I'm starting to see more exploratory frameworks—"two-lane" assessment models, explicitly "AI-infused" courses, co-constructed guidelines with students, etc.

Students are learning about AI primarily from peers and social media. Adults are learning in a slower, more considered way, mostly from mainstream media and fellow educators. They are more reluctant to share with each other.

Schools would be smart to take seriously this recommendation from The Rithm Project's survey of 2,600 teenagers: "Non-judgmental intergenerational conversation may be the most important intervention available.

This is accurate. I wrote every word of the published post. However, Pangram has no ability to capture or evaluate the 25,000-word interaction I had with Claude to prepare that post, which included brainstorming and web search and feedback and editing. Pangram might be good at detecting AI content, but it can't detect AI influence.

Chances are, AI can or soon will be able to do the thing we need it to do. The question I build these workshops around is "Should AI do this?" What and how we delegate is a core AI question for schools.
Schools that talk AND decide are making progress in a way that schools that just talk or schools that just decide are not.
